1: At twenty past seven on the morning of the third of October 1962, a boy of fifteen named Renzo Bellini was given a brown paper parcel about the size of a shoebox, an address written on a torn piece of card, and three instructions. Deliver it by hand. Deliver it to the person named and to nobody else. Do not use the tram. The third instruction was the one that mattered and it was not explained to him, because the woman giving it to him was his mother's employer's housekeeper and did not explain things to boys, and because the reason was that the tram fare was forty lire and forty lire was needed for something else that week. Renzo was not told what was in the parcel. He did not ask; in 1962, in that household, a fifteen-year-old did not enquire into a job given to him by a woman of that rank. He put it under his arm, looked at the card, which said a street name and the number twenty-two and a surname, and worked out that it was somewhere north of the river and probably an hour's walk, and set off at half past seven with the whole thing seeming entirely straightforward. The address did not exist. Not in the sense of being hard to find — in the sense that there was no number twenty-two on that street, because that street stopped at number sixteen and had done since before the war. The housekeeper had copied it out of a letter and had written the number of the house it had been sent from rather than the one it was going to, which is the kind of error nobody notices until somebody is standing in the road. He established all this at ten past nine, and what he did about it is the reason anybody knows his name.
2: By half past nine he had done the sensible things and they had not worked. He had walked the whole length of the street twice, on both sides. He had found number sixteen, which was a shuttered workshop, and the last building past it, which had no number on it at all and turned out to be the back of a laundry that fronted onto a different street. He had asked four people. Two did not know, one gave him directions to a street with a similar name on the other side of the district — and this is the thing about asking strangers for an address, which is that the useless answers are delivered with the same confidence as the useful ones and cost the same walk. One told him with total confidence that number twenty-two was there and pointed at the laundry, which is the kind of help that costs an hour. He went to the similarly named street, which took thirty-five minutes, and it had a number twenty-two, and the people in it had never heard the surname on the card. It was now half past ten. A sensible boy goes home at this point. The parcel was not his, the address was wrong through no fault of his, and the woman who gave it to him would have accepted that without much interest and probably without even looking up. Nothing would have happened to him. Nobody would have thought less of him, because nobody would have thought about it at all. He did not go home, and when he was asked about it thirty-odd years later he said the reason was not determination and was certainly not virtue. It was that he had been told not to come back with it, and he was fifteen, and he had taken that literally.
3: Between half past ten and one o'clock he did the thing that turns this from an errand into a nine-hour walk, which is that he stopped searching the street and started working the problem. The distinction sounds small and is not. Up to half past ten he was looking for a building; after it he was looking for a family, which is a different search with different places to look in it. He reasoned that a surname is easier to find than a number. He went to the parish church nearest the first street and asked, and the priest was out. He went to a bar on the corner and asked the man behind it, who did not know but suggested the tobacconist, because tobacconists know everybody. The tobacconist knew the name — knew it well enough to say it back to him with the correct stress on the second syllable — and said that they had moved, and did not know where to, and thought it had been a couple of years ago. That was, in a nine-hour day, the most valuable thing anybody told him, and it took forty seconds, and Renzo very nearly did not go into the shop at all because he had no money to buy anything and felt he could not walk in and simply ask. He described that hesitation, decades later, as the closest he came to failing. He stood outside the door working out whether it was allowed, and then went in and asked, and the man answered him pleasantly and completely and went back to his newspaper. That is the whole of the tobacconist's part in this. He never knew he had been the hinge of anybody's day, and he is in the story only because Renzo, who forgot a great deal else, remembered the stress on that second syllable.
4: The afternoon was worse. He had a name and the fact of a move and nothing else, and he spent from one until about four o'clock doing what you have to do in a city in 1962 without a telephone or any money, which is walking to places where lists are kept and asking people whether he might look at them. He was turned away three times, twice politely. He tried the parish again and the priest was back and was helpful and had no record, because the family had not been parishioners. He tried a second church. He tried the offices of the district, where a clerk explained that the register was not for the public and then, after looking at him for a moment, went and checked it himself and came back and said there were four families of that name in the city and read out the districts they were in without the street numbers, which was probably against the rules and was as far as the man was willing to go. Four districts. Renzo had walked, by this point, something over twenty kilometres, and it was four in the afternoon, and he had eaten nothing since before seven, and he had four districts and no way of narrowing them except by going to each one and asking. He sat down on a wall for ten minutes at about this point, which is the only rest he recorded in the whole day, and worked out the order to do them in. Not the nearest first. He picked the one where a family who had moved from that street would most plausibly have gone, on the basis of rents. He was wrong about the first and right about the second, which is a better strike rate than the four adults who gave him directions that morning.
5: He got it on the second. Not by cleverness — by the ordinary method, which was to go to the district, find the nearest bar to the middle of it, and ask. The first district had taken an hour and produced a woman who thought she knew the name and then decided she did not. The second took eleven minutes. This time the man knew, and knew the street, and it was two streets away, and by twenty past five on the third of October 1962 Renzo Bellini was standing outside the correct door with a parcel that had been under his arm for ten hours and had begun, at some point in the afternoon, to feel like the only fixed thing in the world. He had rehearsed what he was going to say. He had rehearsed it, by his own account, about forty times during the afternoon and had refined it down to one sentence, because the instruction had been to hand it to the person named and he was extremely conscious that after ten hours he might get it wrong at the last moment by mumbling. The sentence gave his name, his mother's employer's name and the name on the card, in that order, and ended by asking whether he had the right person. He knocked. There was a wait of the length that tells you somebody is coming from a long way inside the flat. And then the door opened, and it was not the person on the card, and Renzo, who had been holding one sentence in his head since two o'clock, said it anyway, exactly as rehearsed, to a woman he had never seen before in his life. He got through the whole thing without a mistake, and it is the only part of the day he ever admitted being proud of.
6: She was English, or foreign in some way he could not place, and very thin, and she listened to the whole sentence to the end without interrupting him, which he noticed at the time and mentioned every time he told it afterward, because adults did not generally do that to a delivery boy and he had expected to be stopped halfway through. Then she said that the person named was her housekeeper's sister, that she did did not live here but came on Thursdays, and that today, as he had perhaps not noticed, was a Wednesday. Renzo said afterward that he had understood, in that moment, with total clarity, that he had walked across Rome for ten hours to arrive one day early at a door belonging to a person who was not the person, and that the correct thing to do was hand it over and go home, and that he could not make himself do it, because the instruction had been to the person named and to nobody else. So he stood there holding it. He was fifteen. He had walked thirty kilometres. He said he was not upset and was not being stubborn on purpose; the instruction simply had not got any smaller during the day, and he could not find the part of himself that was willing to bend it. What he did not know, and could not have known, was that he had said all of this out loud. He thought he had stood there in silence. She told him later, in the kitchen, that he had explained the entire instruction to her on the doorstep in one long unbroken sentence, twice, and that the second time was slower than the first. She looked at him for a moment and then said, all right, and asked him whether he had eaten.
7: What happened next took about an hour and a half and is the part he told least often, because it embarrassed him. She brought him into the kitchen and gave him bread and cold chicken and a great deal of water, and did not ask him any questions while he was eating, which he thought at the time was because she was not interested and understood later was the opposite. He ate a great deal. He apologised for how much and she told him not to, in a way he described as brisk rather than kind, and he said the briskness was the thing that made it bearable. When he had finished she asked him to explain the day, and he did, and it took a while because he had to go back and account for the wrong street and the tobacconist and the districts, and she listened to all of it. Then she made him an offer he found so surprising he made her repeat it. She said she would keep the parcel in the hall, unopened, and hand it to the person named when she came on Thursday, and that if he preferred he could come back tomorrow and do it himself, and that either was fine, and that it was entirely his decision because it was his instruction and not hers. He said afterward that no adult had ever put a decision to him in those terms in his life. He thought about it for what he estimated afterward was the better part of a minute, standing in a stranger's kitchen with a plate in front of him, and said he would come back tomorrow. She said that was sensible, and did not argue, and did not point out that it meant another two hours of walking, and he was grateful for that for about thirty years before he worked out that it was deliberate.
8: He came back on the Thursday and handed the parcel to the person named, who thanked him briefly and did not seem to find any of it remarkable, and thanked him a second time at the door, and that is the actual end of the errand. Two days, about thirty-eight kilometres, one parcel across a city a tram would have crossed in twenty minutes. He never found out what was in it. He did not ask then and he did not ask later and he said the not knowing had stopped bothering him by about 1970. He learned who the thin woman was some years afterward, from a magazine, and his reaction was not excitement. He said it made him feel slightly ill for about a week, because he had been in her kitchen with his shoes off, talking for half an hour about a tobacconist. He never contacted her. He was asked, in the nineties, why not, and said that the honest answer was that there had been nothing to contact her about, and that people who make a friendship out of ninety minutes in a kitchen have usually made it up. He told the story to his own children twice and to an interviewer once, in 1996, and the point he made all three times was the same one and it was not about her. It was that a boy of fifteen had walked thirty kilometres to obey an instruction that turned out not to have mattered in the slightest, since the parcel would have reached the same person on the same Thursday either way, and that he had never once, in fifty years, wished he had gone home at half past ten. This story is a work of fiction. Renzo, the parcel, the errand and every detail in it are invented, created for storytelling and not drawn from any record.
